citations.quote:
Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Work in category
$\mathcal O$ with the conventions of the preceding definitions. For a weight
$\lambda$ write $\chi_\lambda$ for the generalized central character obtained
from $\lambda$, so that $\chi_\lambda=\chi_\mu$ if and only if
$\mu\in W\mathbin\cdot\lambda$
([[cor-central-characters-are-dot-weyl-orbits]]), and let
$\mathcal O=\bigoplus_\chi\mathcal O_\chi$ be the central-character
decomposition of [[thm-category-o-decomposes-by-generalized-central-character]]
with inclusions $\operatorname{incl}_\chi$ and exact projections
$\operatorname{pr}_\chi$, so that
$\operatorname{pr}_\chi\circ\operatorname{incl}_\chi=\operatorname{id}$.

For a finite-dimensional $\mathfrak h$-semisimple $\mathfrak g$-module $E$
([[def-weight-and-weight-space-of-a-lie-algebra-representation]]) and two
generalized central characters $\chi,\chi'$, set
$$T_{\chi,E,\chi'}:=\operatorname{pr}_{\chi'}\circ(E\otimes-)\circ\operatorname{incl}_\chi\colon\mathcal O_\chi\longrightarrow\mathcal O_{\chi'}.$$
This is well defined because $E\otimes-$ is an exact endofunctor of
$\mathcal O$
([[prop-tensoring-with-a-finite-dimensional-module-preserves-category-o]])
and the projections and inclusions are exact.

For weights $\lambda,\mu$ with $\mu-\lambda$ integral
([[def-dot-action-facets-and-single-wall-translation-data]]), let $\nu$ be the
unique dominant weight in the linear Weyl orbit $W(\mu-\lambda)$, which exists
and is unique by [[lem-finite-weyl-closed-chambers-and-stabilizers]] and is
integral; let $L(\nu)$ be the finite-dimensional simple module of highest
weight $\nu$
([[thm-finite-dimensional-simple-modules-are-classified-by-dominant-highest-weights]]).
Define
$$T_\lambda^\mu:=T_{\chi_\lambda,L(\nu),\chi_\mu}\colon\mathcal O_{\chi_\lambda}\longrightarrow\mathcal O_{\chi_\mu},\qquad T_\mu^\lambda:=T_{\chi_\mu,L(\nu)^*,\chi_\lambda}\colon\mathcal O_{\chi_\mu}\longrightarrow\mathcal O_{\chi_\lambda},$$
where $L(\nu)^*$ is the ordinary linear dual, a finite-dimensional
$\mathfrak h$-semisimple simple module isomorphic to $L(-w_0\nu)$ by
[[prop-highest-weight-of-the-dual-representation]].

The labels $\lambda$ and $\mu$ denote actual weights and not $\rho$-shifted
parameters. The central-character subcategories used here are those of the
published decomposition; a central-character summand can contain several
linkage blocks of
[[thm-central-character-summands-split-into-linkage-blocks]], while for an
indecomposable central-character summand the present functors are translation
between that summand and its target.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mathfrak g$ be a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra with Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$, a chosen positive-root system and corresponding Borel, Weyl group $W$, and half-sum $\rho$ of positive roots. Let $\chi_\lambda$ and $\chi_\mu$ be the central characters obtained from highest weights $\lambda,\mu\in\mathfrak h^*$ for this Borel. Then

$$\chi_\lambda=\chi_\mu \quad \text{if and only if} \quad \mu\in W\cdot \lambda,$$

where $W\cdot \lambda:=\{w(\lambda+\rho)-\rho : w\in W\}$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). For every
finite-dimensional $\mathfrak h$-semisimple $\mathfrak g$-module $E$ the
translation functor $T_{\chi,E,\chi'}$
([[def-translation-functor-between-o-blocks]]) is exact, and
$T_{\chi',E^*,\chi}$ is both a left and a right adjoint of
$T_{\chi,E,\chi'}$; in particular both functors send projectives to
projectives and injectives to injectives. Consequently, in the setting of
[[def-translation-functor-between-o-blocks]], $T_\mu^\lambda$ is both a left
and a right adjoint of $T_\lambda^\mu$, and the two functors are exact.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $E$ be a
finite-dimensional $\mathfrak h$-semisimple $\mathfrak g$-module with weight
multiplicities $\dim E_\eta$
([[def-weight-and-weight-space-of-a-lie-algebra-representation]]). For every
weight $\mu$, the object $E\otimes\Delta(\mu)$ has a finite Verma flag
([[def-verma-flag-and-its-multiplicities]]) whose factors are $\Delta(\mu+\eta)$,
the factor $\Delta(\mu+\eta)$ occurring $\dim E_\eta$ times; the factors can be
ordered so that a real-linear height $\ell$ with $\ell(\alpha_i)=1$ is nonincreasing.

Consequently, if $X\in\mathcal O$ has a finite Verma flag with multiplicities
$(X:\Delta(\nu))$, then $E\otimes X$ has a finite Verma flag and
$$(E\otimes X:\Delta(\mu))=\sum_\eta\dim E_\eta\,(X:\Delta(\mu-\eta)).$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Work in the real span
$E$ of the roots with its $W$-invariant positive definite form, and let $\xi$
and $\eta$ be weights in $E$ that are dominant, so
$\langle\xi,\alpha_i^\vee\rangle\ge0$ and
$\langle\eta,\alpha_i^\vee\rangle\ge0$ for every simple root $\alpha_i$
([[def-integral-dominant-and-strictly-dominant-weights]]). Then
$$\lvert\xi-w\eta\rvert\ge\lvert\xi-\eta\rvert\qquad\text{for every }w\in W,$$
and equality holds if and only if $w\eta$ lies in the set
$W_\xi\eta=\{v\eta:v\in W_\xi\}$, where $W_\xi=\{v\in W:v\xi=\xi\}$ is the
stabilizer of $\xi$. In particular, if $\xi$ is regular, so that
$W_\xi=\{1\}$, then equality forces $w\eta=\eta$; if $\xi=0$ then equality
holds for every $w$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $\nu$ be a dominant
integral weight
([[def-integral-dominant-and-strictly-dominant-weights]]) and let $\gamma$ be
a weight of the finite-dimensional simple module $L(\nu)$
([[thm-finite-dimensional-simple-modules-are-classified-by-dominant-highest-weights]]).
Then, in the $W$-invariant positive definite form on the real span $E$ of the
roots ([[prop-the-roots-form-a-reduced-crystallographic-euclidean-root-system]]),
$$\lvert\gamma\rvert\le\lvert\nu\rvert,$$
with equality if and only if $\gamma$ lies in the Weyl orbit $W\nu$; moreover
every weight in $W\nu$ occurs in $L(\nu)$ with multiplicity one.
For all weights $\lambda,\mu$, $\dim\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak g}(M(\mu),M(\lambda))\leq1$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Every projective object
of $\mathcal O$ has a finite Verma flag
([[def-verma-flag-and-its-multiplicities]]).

More precisely, each projective cover $P(\mu)$ produced by
[[thm-category-o-has-enough-projectives]] is a direct summand of the
projective object $\operatorname{pr}_C(E\otimes M(\lambda))$ of
[[lem-finite-dimensional-tensors-reach-every-block-simple]], which is a
direct summand of $E\otimes M(\lambda)$; a general projective object has
finite length, hence is a finite direct sum of indecomposable projectives,
each of which is a projective cover of its simple head.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Every simple object
$L(\mu)$ of $\mathcal O$ admits a projective cover
$P(\mu)\twoheadrightarrow L(\mu)$
([[def-essential-epimorphism-and-projective-cover]]), which may be chosen
inside the linkage class of $\mu$; the cover is unique up to isomorphism and
indecomposable. Consequently $\mathcal O$ has enough projectives: every object
of $\mathcal O$ is a quotient of a finite direct sum of such projective
covers, because objects of $\mathcal O$ have finite length and each composition
factor is a quotient of its projective cover.

Fix a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$, a Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$, and a positive Borel $\mathfrak b=\mathfrak h\oplus\mathfrak n^+$. Write $Q^+=\sum_i\mathbb Z_{\geq0}\alpha_i$, $\mu\leq\lambda$ when $\lambda-\mu\in Q^+$, and $w\cdot\lambda=w(\lambda+\rho)-\rho$.

The category $\mathcal O$ is closed under submodules, quotients and finite direct sums and is an abelian category. If $0\to A\to E\to B\to0$ is exact, $A,B\in\mathcal O$, and $E$ is $\mathfrak h$-semisimple, then $E\in\mathcal O$. The middle-term weight hypothesis is essential.

Every finite-dimensional simple $\mathfrak g$-module is a cyclic highest-weight module whose highest weight is dominant integral, and for each dominant integral weight

$$\lambda=\sum_{i=1}^r m_i\omega_i \qquad (m_i\in \mathbb N_0),$$

there exists, up to isomorphism, a unique finite-dimensional simple module $L(\lambda)$ with highest weight $\lambda$.

Fix a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$ of type
$A_{n-1}$ with Cartan $\mathfrak h$, positive system $\Phi^+$, Weyl vector
$\rho$, Weyl group $W$ (identified with $S_n$) and dot action
$w\cdot\lambda=w(\lambda+\rho)-\rho$. Fix a dominant regular integral weight
$\lambda$, i.e. $\langle\lambda+\rho,\alpha^\vee\rangle\neq0$ for every root and
$\lambda$ integral, and let $\mathcal O_\lambda$ be the corresponding regular
integral block in the conventions of
[[def-regular-integral-category-o-block-and-its-antidominant-weight]]: standard
objects $\Delta(w\cdot\lambda)=M(w\cdot\lambda)$, simples $L(w\cdot\lambda)$,
indecomposable projectives $P(w\cdot\lambda)$ for $w\in W$, with
$\lambda=e\cdot\lambda$ the unique dominant and $w_0\cdot\lambda$ the unique
antidominant element and $\Delta(w_0\cdot\lambda)=L(w_0\cdot\lambda)$.

This item freezes the following conventions, each inherited from the cited
suppliers and used verbatim below.

(i) **Multiplicity conventions.** $(P(w\cdot\lambda):\Delta(y\cdot\lambda))$ is
the Verma-flag multiplicity of [[def-verma-flag-and-its-multiplicities]] and
$[M(y\cdot\lambda):L(w\cdot\lambda)]$ the composition multiplicity, and
$$(P(w\cdot\lambda):\Delta(y\cdot\lambda))=[M(y\cdot\lambda):L(w\cdot\lambda)]$$
by BGG reciprocity ([[thm-bgg-reciprocity]]).

(ii) **Bruhat reversal convention.** Along the bijection
$W\ni w\mapsto w\cdot\lambda$ the Bruhat order runs opposite to the dominance
order, in the two exact senses used on this page: $y\le w$ implies
$w\cdot\lambda\le y\cdot\lambda$ in the dominance order, and every nonzero
multiplicity forces the index direction, i.e.
$[M(y\cdot\lambda):L(w\cdot\lambda)]\neq0$ implies $y\le w$ in the Bruhat
order. The first sense is the inclusion direction of
[[lem-dominant-integral-dot-translates-embed-in-the-verma-module]] (for
$w\ge y$ one has $M(w\cdot\lambda)\subseteq M(y\cdot\lambda)$, so the highest
weight of the submodule is the lower one), and the second is
[[lem-jordan-holder-factors-of-verma-modules-lie-above-the-head]], which
confines every composition factor of $M(y\cdot\lambda)$ to labels
$w\ge y$. The full statement that the two orders are isomorphic as posets is
not needed here and is not asserted; only these two directions, together with
the finiteness of intervals of the Bruhat order
([[lem-bruhat-order-basic-properties-for-permutations]]), are used.

(iii) **Hecke and Kazhdan–Lusztig normalization.** The Kazhdan–Lusztig basis
$\underline H_w=\sum_{y\le w}p_{y,w}H_y$ of the normalized type-$A$ Hecke
algebra ([[thm-existence-and-uniqueness-of-the-kazhdan-lusztig-basis]]), with
$$p_{y,w}=v^{\ell(w)-\ell(y)}P_{y,w}(v^{-2})$$
in the classical $q=v^{-2}$ normalization
([[def-kazhdan-lusztig-polynomials-in-the-classical-q-normalization]]), support
$p_{y,w}=0$ unless $y\le w$, diagonal $p_{w,w}=1$, and simultaneous inversion
symmetry $p_{y^{-1},w^{-1}}=p_{y,w}$.

(iv) **Soergel label and character dictionary.** Write $R_x$ for the
polynomial standard graph bimodule supported at $x$, and $B_x$ for the
normalized indecomposable polynomial Soergel bimodule, which is generally not a
standard graph bimodule. With right reduction $\bar B=B\otimes_S\mathbb C$
and left coinvariant-module values of $V$, the projective dictionary is
$$V(P(w\cdot\lambda))\cong\bar B_{w^{-1}}$$
([[thm-indecomposable-projectives-correspond-to-indecomposable-soergel-modules]]).
The graph label $x$ corresponds to the standard
$\Delta(x^{-1}\cdot\lambda)$. The individual support ranks are measured on the
polynomial lift before reduction, as in
[[prop-verma-flag-multiplicities-are-standard-filtration-ranks-under-v]];
no separated graph-support filtration of the reduced module is asserted.

For degree bookkeeping use precisely the standard-generator normalization of
[[def-type-a-standard-graph-bimodules-support-filtrations-and-character]]:
$\Delta_x(d)=R_x(d-\ell(x))$, and $r_{x,d}(B)$ counts these normalized polynomial
standard layers. Thus the coefficient polynomial is
$$m_x(B;v):=\sum_d r_{x,d}(B)v^d,\qquad h_\Delta(B)=\sum_xm_x(B;v)\widetilde T_x,\qquad\widetilde T_x=v^{\ell(x)}T_x.$$
Here $\widetilde T_x$ is the normalized **standard** Hecke element $H_x$ used
in clause (iii) and
[[def-normalized-type-a-hecke-algebra-and-its-bar-involution]]. The published
Soergel split-Grothendieck-ring convention instead names its simple
Kazhdan--Lusztig generators $H_i=v(T_i+1)=\widetilde T_{s_i}+v$; these must not
be confused with the standard element $H_{s_i}=vT_i$
([[thm-split-grothendieck-group-of-the-soergel-category-is-the-type-a-hecke-algebra]]).
The standard-character supplier
[[lem-the-type-a-standard-character-is-multiplicative]] identifies $h_\Delta$
with that split-Grothendieck-ring isomorphism. This records the coefficient
normalization, and does not infer the image of a general indecomposable $B_x$
by multiplying simple generators. In particular the character theorem must be
used to identify $h_\Delta(B_x)$ with $\underline H_x$; a product of simple
Soergel classes is a Bott--Samelson class and need not be $[B_x]$.
The inverse labels and all rank comparisons above use auxiliary polynomial
gradings only; forgetting them gives the ordinary projective dictionary.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. In a regular integral type-$A$ block
$\mathcal O_\lambda$, for all $y,w\in W$
$$(P(w\cdot\lambda):\Delta(y\cdot\lambda))=P_{y,w}(1),$$
the value at $q=1$ of the classical Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomial of the pair
$y\le w$; the multiplicity is the total value at one, not an individual
coefficient of $P_{y,w}$, and it vanishes unless $y\le w$ in the Bruhat order.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. In a regular integral type-$A$ block
$\mathcal O_\lambda$, for all $y,w\in W$
$$[M(y\cdot\lambda):L(w\cdot\lambda)]=(P(w\cdot\lambda):\Delta(y\cdot\lambda))=P_{y,w}(1),$$
with the pair ordered so that the multiplicity vanishes unless $y\le w$ in the
Bruhat order; in particular the Kazhdan–Lusztig conjecture's multiplicity
statement holds for every dominant regular integral weight, with the same
combinatorial answer.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). For all weights
$\lambda$ and $\mu$,
$$(P(\lambda):\Delta(\mu))=[\Delta(\mu):L(\lambda)]=[M(\mu):L(\lambda)],$$
where $P(\lambda)$ is the projective cover of $L(\lambda)$, the left-hand
multiplicity is the Verma-flag multiplicity of
[[thm-projectives-in-category-o-have-verma-flags]], and the right-hand
multiplicity is the simple composition multiplicity of the Verma module
$M(\mu)$ ([[def-standard-and-costandard-objects-in-category-o]]).

Assume the Axiom of Choice. In a regular integral type-$A$ block
$\mathcal O_\lambda$, for every $w\in W$ the class of $L(w\cdot\lambda)$ in the
Grothendieck group, equivalently its formal character, is
$$[L(w\cdot\lambda)]=\sum_{x\in W}q'_{w,x}(1)\,[M(x\cdot\lambda)],\qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad \mathrm{ch}\,L(w\cdot\lambda)=\sum_{x\in W}q'_{w,x}(1)\,\mathrm{ch}\,M(x\cdot\lambda),$$
where $q'_{x,w}$ are the inverse Kazhdan–Lusztig coefficients of
[[def-inverse-kazhdan-lusztig-polynomials]] ($Q'=P^{-1}$, $q'_{x,w}\in v\mathbb Z[v]$
for $x<w$, $q'_{w,w}=1$) and the sum is supported on $x\ge w$. Equivalently, in
the signed normalization $q_{x,w}=\mathrm{sgn}(x)\mathrm{sgn}(w)q'_{x,w}$ the
formula is the signed inverse-Kazhdan–Lusztig sum
$$\mathrm{ch}\,L(w\cdot\lambda)=\sum_{x\ge w}(-1)^{\ell(w)-\ell(x)}q_{w,x}(1)\,\mathrm{ch}\,M(x\cdot\lambda).$$
The coefficients $q'_{w,x}(1)$ are the weighted incidence-algebra inverse of
$(P_{y,z}(1))$, given by the finite signed chain sum of products of
$P_{y,z}(1)$; they are integers that may be negative. They specialize to
ordinary Bruhat Möbius values on intervals where every comparable-pair
Kazhdan–Lusztig value is $1$, but not in general. Only the value at $q=1$
occurs.

For weights $\lambda,\mu$ with $\mu-\lambda$ integral
([[def-dot-action-facets-and-single-wall-translation-data]]), let $\nu$ be the
unique dominant weight in the linear Weyl orbit $W(\mu-\lambda)$, which exists
and is unique by [[lem-finite-weyl-closed-chambers-and-stabilizers]] and is
integral; let $L(\nu)$ be the finite-dimensional simple module of highest
weight $\nu$
([[thm-finite-dimensional-simple-modules-are-classified-by-dominant-highest-weights]]).
Define
$$T_\lambda^\mu:=T_{\chi_\lambda,L(\nu),\chi_\mu}\colon\mathcal O_{\chi_\lambda}\longrightarrow\mathcal O_{\chi_\mu},\qquad T_\mu^\lambda:=T_{\chi_\mu,L(\nu)^*,\chi_\lambda}\colon\mathcal O_{\chi_\mu}\longrightarrow\mathcal O_{\chi_\lambda},$$
where $L(\nu)^*$ is the ordinary linear dual, a finite-dimensional
$\mathfrak h$-semisimple simple module isomorphic to $L(-w_0\nu)$ by
[[prop-highest-weight-of-the-dual-representation]].

derivations.claim:
Since $\lambda$ and $\mu$ are dominant regular integral, the shifted weights $a=\lambda+ho$ and $b=\mu+ho$ are strictly dominant and have trivial stabilizers in $W$; the dominant member $
u$ of $W(\mu-\lambda)=W(b-a)$ satisfies $|
u|=|b-a|$, and by [F5] and [F10] every weight $\gamma$ of $E=L(
u)$ has $|\gamma|\le|b-a|$, with equality exactly on $W
u$, where the multiplicity is one.

By [F2] the functors $F$ and $G$ are exact, and $G$ is both a left and a right adjoint of $F$ (with the roles of $E$ and $E^*$ exchanged for the reverse pair); exactness of the right adjoint on the other side makes $F$ preserve projectives and $G$ preserve projectives. Write $\eta:\operatorname{Id}\to GF$ and $\varepsilon:FG\to\operatorname{Id}$ for the unit and counit of the adjunction $F\dashv G$; both composites $GF$ and $FG$ are exact as compositions of exact functors.

Compute $F\Delta(y\cdot\lambda)=\operatorname{pr}_{\chi_\mu}(E\otimes\Delta(y\cdot\lambda))$ for $y\in W$. By [F3] the object $E\otimes\Delta(y\cdot\lambda)$ has a Verma flag with factors $\Delta(y\cdot\lambda+\gamma)$, $\gamma$ running over the weights of $E$ with multiplicity $\dim E_\gamma$, and by [F1] the exact projection $\operatorname{pr}_{\chi_\mu}$ maps this flag to a flag of the projected object whose factor at $\gamma$ is $\Delta(y\cdot\lambda+\gamma)$ when $y\cdot\lambda+\gamma\in W\cdot\mu$ and $0$ otherwise. A retained factor has $y\cdot\lambda+\gamma=x\cdot\mu$ for some $x$, that is $ya+\gamma=xb$ with $a,b$ strictly dominant and regular. Then $|\gamma|=|xb-ya|=|b-x^{-1}ya|\ge|b-a|$ by [F4] applied to the dominant vectors $b$ and $a$; regularity of $b$ makes equality of the norm comparison force $x^{-1}ya=a$, and regularity of $a$ then forces $x=y$. Comparing with the bound $|\gamma|\le|b-a|$ of [F5] gives equality, so $\gamma\in W\nu$ and $x=y$; then $\gamma=y(b-a)=y(\mu-\lambda)$, the factor is $\Delta(y\cdot\lambda+y(\mu-\lambda))=\Delta(y\cdot\mu)$, and by the multiplicity-one clause of [F5] it occurs exactly once. No other retained factor exists, since every retained factor was shown to equal this one. The projected object therefore has a one-step flag with quotient $\Delta(y\cdot\mu)$, so $F\Delta(y\cdot\lambda)\cong\Delta(y\cdot\mu)$ for every $y$.

The dual computation gives $G\Delta(y\cdot\mu)\cong\Delta(y\cdot\lambda)$ for every $y$. By [F3] applied to the finite-dimensional module $E^*$ of [F10], the flag factors of $E^*\otimes\Delta(y\cdot\mu)$ are $\Delta(y\cdot\mu+\gamma')$ with multiplicities $\dim(E^*)_{\gamma'}$, and a factor retained by $\operatorname{pr}_{\chi_\lambda}$ satisfies $yb+\gamma'=xa$ for some $x\in W$. Then $|\gamma'|=|xa-yb|=|a-x^{-1}yb|\ge|b-a|$ by [F4] applied to the dominant vectors $a$ and $b$, and regularity of $a$ forces $x^{-1}yb=b$ and then $x=y$; the weight bound [F5] applied to the weights of $E^*$ (whose extremal orbit is $W(\lambda-\mu)$ with multiplicity one, [F10]) gives equality $|\gamma'|=|b-a|$, $\gamma'=y(a-b)=y(\lambda-\mu)$, and the retained factor $\Delta(y\cdot\mu+y(\lambda-\mu))=\Delta(y\cdot\lambda)$ occurs once. Hence $G\Delta(y\cdot\mu)\cong\Delta(y\cdot\lambda)$.

For each $y\in W$, the unit $\eta_{\Delta(y\cdot\lambda)}:\Delta(y\cdot\lambda)\to GF\Delta(y\cdot\lambda)$ corresponds under the adjunction isomorphism $\operatorname{Hom}(F\Delta(y\cdot\lambda),F\Delta(y\cdot\lambda))\cong\operatorname{Hom}(\Delta(y\cdot\lambda),GF\Delta(y\cdot\lambda))$ to the identity of $F\Delta(y\cdot\lambda)$; since $F\Delta(y\cdot\lambda)\cong\Delta(y\cdot\mu)\ne0$ by step 2.1, the unit is nonzero. Its target is $GF\Delta(y\cdot\lambda)\cong G\Delta(y\cdot\mu)\cong\Delta(y\cdot\lambda)$ by steps 2.1 and 2.2, so $\eta_{\Delta(y\cdot\lambda)}$ is a nonzero endomorphism of a Verma module after transport along this isomorphism, and by [F6] every nonzero endomorphism of a Verma module is an isomorphism. Hence $\eta$ is an isomorphism on every standard object of $\mathcal O_\lambda$.

The same argument for the counit: for each $y\in W$, $\varepsilon_{\Delta(y\cdot\mu)}:FG\Delta(y\cdot\mu)\to\Delta(y\cdot\mu)$ corresponds to the identity of $G\Delta(y\cdot\mu)\ne0$ under the adjunction, hence is nonzero, and its source is $FG\Delta(y\cdot\mu)\cong F\Delta(y\cdot\lambda)\cong\Delta(y\cdot\mu)$ by steps 2.1 and 2.2; by [F6] it is an isomorphism on every standard object of $\mathcal O_\mu$.

The isomorphisms of steps 3.1 and 3.2 extend to every Verma-filtered object. If $0\to A\to B\to C\to0$ is a short exact sequence in $\mathcal O_\lambda$ with $A$ and $C$ Verma-filtered and $\eta_A,\eta_C$ isomorphisms, then $GF$ is exact by step 1.2, and naturality of $\eta$ gives a map of short exact sequences from $0\to A\to B\to C\to0$ to $0\to GFA\to GFB\to GFC\to0$ with isomorphisms at the outer terms; the five lemma makes $\eta_B$ an isomorphism. Inducting along a finite Verma flag of $X$ ([[def-verma-flag-and-its-multiplicities]], the flag decomposition $0=X_0\subseteq\cdots\subseteq X_n=X$ with Verma quotients) gives that $\eta_X$ is an isomorphism for every Verma-filtered $X$, and [F7] makes every projective of $\mathcal O_\lambda$ Verma-filtered; the identical induction with $FG$ exact and the counit gives that $\varepsilon_Y$ is an isomorphism for every Verma-filtered $Y$ of $\mathcal O_\mu$, in particular for every projective.

The isomorphisms extend to all objects by finite projective presentations. By [F8] every object $X$ of $\mathcal O_\lambda$ has finite length and is a quotient of a finite direct sum of projective covers; choosing such a cover $P_0\twoheadrightarrow X$ and applying the same to the kernel of this map (an object of $\mathcal O_\lambda$ by [F9]) produces an exact sequence $P_1\to P_0\to X\to0$ with $P_0,P_1$ finite direct sums of projective covers, hence projective and Verma-filtered by [F7]. Applying the exact functor $GF$ and using naturality of $\eta$ identifies $\eta_X$ with the map induced on the cokernel of $\eta_{P_1},\eta_{P_0}$, which are isomorphisms by step 4.1; therefore $\eta_X$ is an isomorphism. The same argument in $\mathcal O_\mu$ with a finite projective presentation and the exact functor $FG$ makes $\varepsilon_Y$ an isomorphism for every $Y$ in $\mathcal O_\mu$. Thus the unit and counit of the adjunction $F\dashv G$ are natural isomorphisms, so $F$ and $G$ are mutually inverse equivalences of categories.

Being inverse equivalences, $F$ is exact and reflects the categorical structures. For the labels: $F\Delta(w\cdot\lambda)\cong\Delta(w\cdot\mu)$ was proved in step 2.1. For each $w$, $FL(w\cdot\lambda)$ is a simple object, and the exact functor $F$ turns the epimorphism $\Delta(w\cdot\lambda)\twoheadrightarrow L(w\cdot\lambda)$ onto its unique simple quotient into an epimorphism $\Delta(w\cdot\mu)\cong F\Delta(w\cdot\lambda)\twoheadrightarrow FL(w\cdot\lambda)$; since the simple quotient of $\Delta(w\cdot\mu)$ is unique and equal to $L(w\cdot\mu)$, one has $FL(w\cdot\lambda)\cong L(w\cdot\mu)$. Finally $P(w\cdot\lambda)$ is a projective cover of $L(w\cdot\lambda)$ by [F8] and [F11], so $FP(w\cdot\lambda)$ is a projective object mapping onto $FL(w\cdot\lambda)\cong L(w\cdot\mu)$ with essential kernel: if a subobject $Z'\subseteq FP(w\cdot\lambda)$ mapped onto $FL(w\cdot\lambda)$, then applying the inverse equivalence would exhibit a subobject of $P(w\cdot\lambda)$ mapping onto $L(w\cdot\lambda)$, so essentiality on the source forces $Z'=FP(w\cdot\lambda)$. By uniqueness of projective covers in [F8], $FP(w\cdot\lambda)\cong P(w\cdot\mu)$. The dual statements $G\Delta(w\cdot\mu)\cong\Delta(w\cdot\lambda)$, $GL(w\cdot\mu)\cong L(w\cdot\lambda)$ and $GP(w\cdot\mu)\cong P(w\cdot\lambda)$ follow from step 2.2 and the identical argument with the roles exchanged.

The multiplicities are transported termwise. Since $F$ is an equivalence, it is full and faithful, so applying $F$ to a finite Verma flag of $P$ and applying $G$ to a finite Verma flag of $FP$ are inverse bijections between the flag multiplicities of $P$ and of $FP$; by steps 6.1 and 2.2 the labels match, giving $(FP(w\cdot\lambda):F\Delta(y\cdot\lambda))=(P(w\cdot\lambda):\Delta(y\cdot\lambda))$ and, with step 6.1, $(P(w\cdot\mu):\Delta(y\cdot\mu))=(P(w\cdot\lambda):\Delta(y\cdot\lambda))=P_{y,w}(1)$ by [F11]; BGG reciprocity [F11] likewise transports the composition multiplicities and their vanishing. Transporting the identity of [F12] along the induced isomorphism of Grothendieck groups gives $[L(w\cdot\mu)]=\sum_xq'_{w,x}(1)[M(x\cdot\mu)]$ with the same weighted-inverse coefficients and the same support $x\ge w$, because $F$ carries $L(w\cdot\lambda)$ to $L(w\cdot\mu)$ and $M(x\cdot\lambda)=\Delta(x\cdot\lambda)$ to $M(x\cdot\mu)$. The conventions are preserved because the label $w$ is unchanged: dominant and antidominant labels, Bruhat comparisons, left/right labels and inverse Soergel labels carry over; the formal characters are read in the respective weight series $x\cdot\lambda$ and $x\cdot\mu$ and need not coincide. Nothing above uses or produces a grading on $\mathcal O$, an $\mathrm{Ext}$-algebra or a Koszul structure.

boundaries.evidence: Step 4.1's induction runs over finite Verma flags and includes the empty flag: for the zero object both unit and counit are isomorphisms because GF and FG are additive and F, G are exact by step 1.2.

Vanishing cases are asserted, not skipped: step 2.1 shows every non-retained Verma factor contributes 0 under the block projection, and step 7.1 transports flag multiplicities including the zero ones.
The single-factor case is the standard computation of steps 2.1 and 2.2: F Delta(y.lambda) = Delta(y.mu) is a one-factor statement, and step 4.1's induction starts from it.

boundaries.reason: Both weights are dominant regular integral, so no wall crossing or singular facet occurs; translation functors cease to be equivalences at singular parameters, and that regime is outside the statement.

boundaries.evidence: The endpoint labels e and w_0 are inside step 6.1's 'for every w in W': F Delta(e.lambda) = Delta(e.mu) is the dominant standard and F Delta(w_0.lambda) = Delta(w_0.mu) the antidominant one.
AC is assumed in the Statement; step 5.1 consumes it through the finite projective presentations and cover theory of [F8], and the equivalence constructed there inherits the assumption explicitly.
Step 6.1 proves the forward label transport: F sends Delta(w.lambda), L(w.lambda), P(w.lambda) to the labelled objects over mu.
Step 6.1 also proves the converse transport for G, so both directions of the equivalence are recorded and no converse is left implicit.

(iv) **Soergel label and character dictionary.** Write $R_x$ for the
polynomial standard graph bimodule supported at $x$, and $B_x$ for the
normalized indecomposable polynomial Soergel bimodule, which is generally not a
standard graph bimodule. With right reduction $\bar B=B\otimes_S\mathbb C$
and left coinvariant-module values of $V$, the projective dictionary is
$$V(P(w\cdot\lambda))\cong\bar B_{w^{-1}}$$
([[thm-indecomposable-projectives-correspond-to-indecomposable-soergel-modules]]).
The graph label $x$ corresponds to the standard
$\Delta(x^{-1}\cdot\lambda)$. The individual support ranks are measured on the
polynomial lift before reduction, as in
[[prop-verma-flag-multiplicities-are-standard-filtration-ranks-under-v]];
no separated graph-support filtration of the reduced module is asserted.

For degree bookkeeping use precisely the standard-generator normalization of
[[def-type-a-standard-graph-bimodules-support-filtrations-and-character]]:
$\Delta_x(d)=R_x(d-\ell(x))$, and $r_{x,d}(B)$ counts these normalized polynomial
standard layers. Thus the coefficient polynomial is
$$m_x(B;v):=\sum_d r_{x,d}(B)v^d,\qquad h_\Delta(B)=\sum_xm_x(B;v)\widetilde T_x,\qquad\widetilde T_x=v^{\ell(x)}T_x.$$
Here $\widetilde T_x$ is the normalized **standard** Hecke element $H_x$ used
in clause (iii) and
[[def-normalized-type-a-hecke-algebra-and-its-bar-involution]]. The published
Soergel split-Grothendieck-ring convention instead names its simple
Kazhdan--Lusztig generators $H_i=v(T_i+1)=\widetilde T_{s_i}+v$; these must not
be confused with the standard element $H_{s_i}=vT_i$
([[thm-split-grothendieck-group-of-the-soergel-category-is-the-type-a-hecke-algebra]]).
The standard-character supplier
[[lem-the-type-a-standard-character-is-multiplicative]] identifies $h_\Delta$
with that split-Grothendieck-ring isomorphism. This records the coefficient
normalization, and does not infer the image of a general indecomposable $B_x$
by multiplying simple generators. In particular the character theorem must be
used to identify $h_\Delta(B_x)$ with $\underline H_x$; a product of simple
Soergel classes is a Bott--Samelson class and need not be $[B_x]$.
The inverse labels and all rank comparisons above use auxiliary polynomial
gradings only; forgetting them gives the ordinary projective dictionary.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mathfrak g$ be a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra with Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$, a chosen positive-root system and corresponding Borel, Weyl group $W$, and half-sum $\rho$ of positive roots. Let $\chi_\lambda$ and $\chi_\mu$ be the central characters obtained from highest weights $\lambda,\mu\in\mathfrak h^*$ for this Borel. Then

$$\chi_\lambda=\chi_\mu \quad \text{if and only if} \quad \mu\in W\cdot \lambda,$$

where $W\cdot \lambda:=\{w(\lambda+\rho)-\rho : w\in W\}$.

For $\lambda\in\mathfrak h^*$, the **Verma module** is the induced
$\mathfrak g$-module

$$M(\lambda):=U(\mathfrak g)\otimes_{U(\mathfrak b)}\mathbb C_\lambda,$$

where $U(\mathfrak g)$ is the quotient algebra of
[[def-universal-enveloping-algebra-as-a-tensor-quotient]] and
$\mathbb C_\lambda$ is [[def-one-dimensional-borel-module-of-weight-lambda]].
Write $v_\lambda:=1\otimes c_\lambda$.  Thus $M(\lambda)$ is the quotient of
$U(\mathfrak g)$ by the left ideal generated by $x$ for $x\in\mathfrak n^+$
and $h-\lambda(h)$ for $h\in\mathfrak h$; in particular,
$\mathfrak n^+v_\lambda=0$ and $hv_\lambda=\lambda(h)v_\lambda$.

Multiplication gives a vector-space isomorphism

$$U(\mathfrak n^-)\xrightarrow{\sim}M(\lambda),\qquad u\longmapsto uv_\lambda.$$

Consequently, ordered negative-root PBW monomials from
[[thm-pbw-ordered-monomial-basis-for-the-enveloping-algebra]] applied to
$v_\lambda$ form a basis.

Assume the Axiom of Choice.

If $\langle\lambda+\rho,\alpha^\vee\rangle<0$ for every $\alpha\in\Phi^+$, then $M(\lambda)$ is simple. Thus every regular antidominant weight, in this explicit sense, has simple Verma module.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $\Gamma$ be a
finite downward-closed ideal of a linkage class $C$
([[def-truncated-category-o-at-a-finite-weight-ideal]]) and let
$\lambda\in\Gamma$ be maximal in $\Gamma$. Then $\Delta(\lambda)=M(\lambda)$
is a projective object of the truncation $\mathcal O_\Gamma$
([[def-projective-object]]).

More precisely, for every $X\in\mathcal O_\Gamma$ evaluation at the
highest-weight generator $v_\lambda$ is a natural isomorphism
$\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal O_\Gamma}(M(\lambda),X)\to
X^{\mathfrak n^+}_\lambda=X_\lambda$, and $X\mapsto X_\lambda$ is exact, so
$\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal O_\Gamma}(M(\lambda),-)$ is exact.

Under the fixed positive-Borel convention the essential hypothesis is
maximality of $\lambda$ in the finite ideal $\Gamma$: maximality, not any
antidominance or sufficient-positivity condition, is what makes every
$\lambda$-weight vector singular. For a weight $\lambda$ that is not maximal
in $\Gamma$, $\Delta(\lambda)$ need not be projective in $\mathcal O_\Gamma$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Every simple object
$L(\mu)$ of $\mathcal O$ admits a projective cover
$P(\mu)\twoheadrightarrow L(\mu)$
([[def-essential-epimorphism-and-projective-cover]]), which may be chosen
inside the linkage class of $\mu$; the cover is unique up to isomorphism and
indecomposable. Consequently $\mathcal O$ has enough projectives: every object
of $\mathcal O$ is a quotient of a finite direct sum of such projective
covers, because objects of $\mathcal O$ have finite length and each composition
factor is a quotient of its projective cover.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). For all weights
$\lambda$ and $\mu$,
$$(P(\lambda):\Delta(\mu))=[\Delta(\mu):L(\lambda)]=[M(\mu):L(\lambda)],$$
where $P(\lambda)$ is the projective cover of $L(\lambda)$, the left-hand
multiplicity is the Verma-flag multiplicity of
[[thm-projectives-in-category-o-have-verma-flags]], and the right-hand
multiplicity is the simple composition multiplicity of the Verma module
$M(\mu)$ ([[def-standard-and-costandard-objects-in-category-o]]).

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $\lambda\in\Lambda^+$ and $w\in W$. If a simple module $L(\mu)$ occurs in a composition series of $M(w\circ\lambda)$, then $\mu=u\circ\lambda$ for some $u\ge w$ in Bruhat order; moreover $L(w\circ\lambda)$ occurs exactly once. Consequently every composition factor of $M(w\circ\lambda)$ has length at least $\ell(w)$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Work in category
$\mathcal O$ with the conventions of the preceding definitions. For a weight
$\lambda$ write $\chi_\lambda$ for the generalized central character obtained
from $\lambda$, so that $\chi_\lambda=\chi_\mu$ if and only if
$\mu\in W\mathbin\cdot\lambda$
([[cor-central-characters-are-dot-weyl-orbits]]), and let
$\mathcal O=\bigoplus_\chi\mathcal O_\chi$ be the central-character
decomposition of [[thm-category-o-decomposes-by-generalized-central-character]]
with inclusions $\operatorname{incl}_\chi$ and exact projections
$\operatorname{pr}_\chi$, so that
$\operatorname{pr}_\chi\circ\operatorname{incl}_\chi=\operatorname{id}$.

For a finite-dimensional $\mathfrak h$-semisimple $\mathfrak g$-module $E$
([[def-weight-and-weight-space-of-a-lie-algebra-representation]]) and two
generalized central characters $\chi,\chi'$, set
$$T_{\chi,E,\chi'}:=\operatorname{pr}_{\chi'}\circ(E\otimes-)\circ\operatorname{incl}_\chi\colon\mathcal O_\chi\longrightarrow\mathcal O_{\chi'}.$$
This is well defined because $E\otimes-$ is an exact endofunctor of
$\mathcal O$
([[prop-tensoring-with-a-finite-dimensional-module-preserves-category-o]])
and the projections and inclusions are exact.

For weights $\lambda,\mu$ with $\mu-\lambda$ integral
([[def-dot-action-facets-and-single-wall-translation-data]]), let $\nu$ be the
unique dominant weight in the linear Weyl orbit $W(\mu-\lambda)$, which exists
and is unique by [[lem-finite-weyl-closed-chambers-and-stabilizers]] and is
integral; let $L(\nu)$ be the finite-dimensional simple module of highest
weight $\nu$
([[thm-finite-dimensional-simple-modules-are-classified-by-dominant-highest-weights]]).
Define
$$T_\lambda^\mu:=T_{\chi_\lambda,L(\nu),\chi_\mu}\colon\mathcal O_{\chi_\lambda}\longrightarrow\mathcal O_{\chi_\mu},\qquad T_\mu^\lambda:=T_{\chi_\mu,L(\nu)^*,\chi_\lambda}\colon\mathcal O_{\chi_\mu}\longrightarrow\mathcal O_{\chi_\lambda},$$
where $L(\nu)^*$ is the ordinary linear dual, a finite-dimensional
$\mathfrak h$-semisimple simple module isomorphic to $L(-w_0\nu)$ by
[[prop-highest-weight-of-the-dual-representation]].

The labels $\lambda$ and $\mu$ denote actual weights and not $\rho$-shifted
parameters. The central-character subcategories used here are those of the
published decomposition; a central-character summand can contain several
linkage blocks of
[[thm-central-character-summands-split-into-linkage-blocks]], while for an
indecomposable central-character summand the present functors are translation
between that summand and its target.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\lambda,\mu$ be dominant regular integral
weights for the same complex type-$A$ semisimple Lie algebra and fixed positive
system. Let $\nu$ be the unique dominant member of $W(\mu-\lambda)$ and
$E=L(\nu)$ the finite-dimensional simple. The actual translation functors
$$F=T_\lambda^\mu=\operatorname{pr}_{\chi_\mu}(E\otimes-)\operatorname{incl}_{\chi_\lambda},\qquad G=T_\mu^\lambda=\operatorname{pr}_{\chi_\lambda}(E^*\otimes-)\operatorname{incl}_{\chi_\mu}$$
are exact mutually inverse equivalences, with natural adjunction isomorphisms
$\operatorname{Id}\cong GF$ and $FG\cong\operatorname{Id}$. They preserve the
dot-orbit labels: for every $w\in W$,
$$F\Delta(w\cdot\lambda)\cong\Delta(w\cdot\mu),\quad FL(w\cdot\lambda)\cong L(w\cdot\mu),\quad FP(w\cdot\lambda)\cong P(w\cdot\mu),$$
and conversely for $G$. Consequently the two blocks have identical Verma-flag
and composition multiplicities, both equal to $P_{y,w}(1)$, and $F$ transports
the inverse-Kazhdan–Lusztig character identity as a Grothendieck-group identity
with the same signed weighted-inverse coefficients $q'_{w,x}(1)$ and the same
support $x\ge w$. Formal characters in the two blocks use their respective
weights $x\cdot\lambda$ and $x\cdot\mu$; they need not be equal as weight
series. The dominant/antidominant, Bruhat, left/right and inverse-Soergel-label
conventions are preserved. This is an ungraded categorical transport and
supplies no Ext or Koszul grading.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $E$ be a
finite-dimensional $\mathfrak h$-semisimple $\mathfrak g$-module with weight
multiplicities $\dim E_\eta$
([[def-weight-and-weight-space-of-a-lie-algebra-representation]]). For every
weight $\mu$, the object $E\otimes\Delta(\mu)$ has a finite Verma flag
([[def-verma-flag-and-its-multiplicities]]) whose factors are $\Delta(\mu+\eta)$,
the factor $\Delta(\mu+\eta)$ occurring $\dim E_\eta$ times; the factors can be
ordered so that a real-linear height $\ell$ with $\ell(\alpha_i)=1$ is nonincreasing.

Consequently, if $X\in\mathcal O$ has a finite Verma flag with multiplicities
$(X:\Delta(\nu))$, then $E\otimes X$ has a finite Verma flag and
$$(E\otimes X:\Delta(\mu))=\sum_\eta\dim E_\eta\,(X:\Delta(\mu-\eta)).$$

Identify $\mathbb Z[q]$ with $\mathbb Z[v^{-2}]$ by $q\mapsto v^{-2}$. For $y\le w$ in $S_n$, put $d=\ell(w)-\ell(y)$ and define the **Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomial** $P_{y,w}(q)\in\mathbb Z[q]$ by $$P_{y,w}(v^{-2})=v^{-d}p_{y,w},$$ where $\underline H_w=\sum_{y\le w}p_{y,w}H_y$ is the Kazhdan–Lusztig basis of [[thm-existence-and-uniqueness-of-the-kazhdan-lusztig-basis]]. The parity clause of that theorem makes the right side a polynomial in $v^{-2}$. The conventions are: $P_{y,w}=0$ unless $y\le w$, $P_{w,w}=1$, $P_{y,w}$ has constant term 1, and for $y<w$ its degree is at most $(\ell(w)-\ell(y)-1)/2$. The **$\mu$-coefficient** is $$\mu(y,w):=	ext{coefficient of }q^{(\ell(w)-\ell(y)-1)/2}	ext{ in }P_{y,w},$$ defined to be 0 when $\ell(w)-\ell(y)$ is even; equivalently $\mu(y,w)$ is the coefficient of $v$ in $p_{y,w}$. One writes $\mu(y|w)
e0$ when $y
e w$ and ($y<w$ and $\mu(y,w)
e0$) or ($w<y$ and $\mu(w,y)
e0$). The dictionary with the literature is recorded for use: with the classical parameter $T_s^2=(q-1)T_s+q$ one has $H_w=v^{\ell(w)}T_w$, the element $\underline H_w$ is the basis element $C'_w$ of [EW], and $h_{y,w}=p_{y,w}$ with $v^{\ell(w)-\ell(y)}P_{y,w}(v^{-2})=h_{y,w}$ [EW, Remark 3.2].

Assume the Axiom of Choice. In a regular integral type-$A$ block
$\mathcal O_\lambda$, for every $w\in W$ the class of $L(w\cdot\lambda)$ in the
Grothendieck group, equivalently its formal character, is
$$[L(w\cdot\lambda)]=\sum_{x\in W}q'_{w,x}(1)\,[M(x\cdot\lambda)],\qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad \mathrm{ch}\,L(w\cdot\lambda)=\sum_{x\in W}q'_{w,x}(1)\,\mathrm{ch}\,M(x\cdot\lambda),$$
where $q'_{x,w}$ are the inverse Kazhdan–Lusztig coefficients of
[[def-inverse-kazhdan-lusztig-polynomials]] ($Q'=P^{-1}$, $q'_{x,w}\in v\mathbb Z[v]$
for $x<w$, $q'_{w,w}=1$) and the sum is supported on $x\ge w$. Equivalently, in
the signed normalization $q_{x,w}=\mathrm{sgn}(x)\mathrm{sgn}(w)q'_{x,w}$ the
formula is the signed inverse-Kazhdan–Lusztig sum
$$\mathrm{ch}\,L(w\cdot\lambda)=\sum_{x\ge w}(-1)^{\ell(w)-\ell(x)}q_{w,x}(1)\,\mathrm{ch}\,M(x\cdot\lambda).$$
The coefficients $q'_{w,x}(1)$ are the weighted incidence-algebra inverse of
$(P_{y,z}(1))$, given by the finite signed chain sum of products of
$P_{y,z}(1)$; they are integers that may be negative. They specialize to
ordinary Bruhat Möbius values on intervals where every comparable-pair
Kazhdan–Lusztig value is $1$, but not in general. Only the value at $q=1$
occurs.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). For every dominant
integral weight $\lambda\in\Lambda^+$, the character of the finite-dimensional
simple module $L(\lambda)$ is
$$\operatorname{ch}L(\lambda)=A(\lambda+\rho)\cdot A(\rho)^{-1}=\Bigl(\sum_{w\in W}(-1)^{\ell(w)}e^{w(\lambda+\rho)}\Bigr)\Big/\Bigl(e^{\rho}\prod_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}(1-e^{-\alpha})\Bigr),$$
the quotient being taken in the completed character ring $\mathcal R$ of
[[def-completed-formal-character-ring-for-downward-cones]], where
$A(\rho)$ is invertible with inverse
$e^{-\rho}\prod_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}(1-e^{-\alpha})^{-1}$
([[thm-weyl-denominator-identity]],
[[lem-geometric-series-invertibility-in-the-completed-character-ring]]). No
quotient of ordinary functions is intended before this formal cancellation is
justified.

derivations.claim: **The two blocks.** With $\rho=1$ the dot action on coordinates is $s\cdot l=s(l+1)-1=-l-2$, so the orbit of $n$ is $\{n,-n-2\}$; a weight $l$ is dominant regular integral exactly when $l\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}$, and then $-n-2<n$ in the dominance order. Hence $C_n$ is a regular integral block with the two labels $e=123\mapsto n$ and $s=213\mapsto-n-2$; for $n=0$ and $n=1$ the abstract labelled data are the same, which is what makes the two blocks directly comparable.

**The PBW computation.** Fix $n\ge0$ and put $v_k:=f^kv_n$, a basis of $M(n)$ by [F2]; the highest weight vector $v_0$ generates $M(n)$ and spans the $n$-weight space, which is one-dimensional. From the $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ relations $[h,f]=-2f$, $[e,f]=h$ one computes $h\cdot v_k=(n-2k)v_k$, $f\cdot v_k=v_{k+1}$, and, by induction on $k$ from $e\cdot v_0=0$, $e\cdot v_k=k(n-k+1)v_{k-1}$. If $M(n)=A\oplus B$ with $v_0=a+b$, then $a$ and $b$ lie in the one-dimensional weight space $M(n)_n=\mathbb Cv_0$; if $b\ne0$ then $b$ is a nonzero multiple of $v_0$, so $v_0\in B$ and $M(n)=U(\mathfrak g)v_0\subseteq B$, while if $b=0$ then $v_0=a\in A$ and $M(n)\subseteq A$; either way one of the summands is zero. So $M(n)$ is indecomposable.

**The submodule $W$.** Let $W:=\operatorname{span}\{v_k:k\ge n+1\}$. By step 1.2 it is stable under $f$ and $h$; and $e\cdot v_{n+1}=(n+1)(n-(n+1)+1)v_n=0$, while for $k\ge n+2$ one has $e\cdot v_k=k(n-k+1)v_{k-1}$ with $k-1\ge n+1$, so $e$ maps $W$ into $W$. Hence $W$ is a nonzero submodule. Its highest weight vector $v_{n+1}$ has weight $n-2(n+1)=-n-2$ and is killed by $e$; the linear map $M(-n-2)\to W$ sending the basis element $f^kv_{-n-2}$ of the PBW model of $M(-n-2)$ to $v_{n+1+k}$ is a $\mathfrak g$-module isomorphism by the action formulas of step 1.2 (both sides have the same $h$-eigenvalues and the same $e,f$-action). Since $-n-2+1=-n-1<0$, the Verma $M(-n-2)$ is simple by [F3], so $W\cong M(-n-2)=L(-n-2)$.

**Characters.** By step 1.2 the weight multiplicities of $M(n)$ are $1$ in each weight $n-2k$, $k\ge0$, so $\mathrm{ch}\,M(n)=\sum_{k\ge0}e^{n-2k}$ and $\mathrm{ch}\,M(-n-2)=\sum_{k\ge0}e^{-n-2-2k}$; the character formula of [F10] therefore gives $\mathrm{ch}\,L(n)=\mathrm{ch}\,M(n)-\mathrm{ch}\,M(-n-2)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}e^{n-2k}=e^{n}+e^{n-2}+\cdots+e^{-n}$, in agreement with the Weyl character of the finite-dimensional simple $L(n)$ by [F11], and $\mathrm{ch}\,L(-n-2)=\mathrm{ch}\,M(-n-2)$.

**The quotient is $L(n)$.** By step 1.2 the images of $v_0,\dots,v_n$ form a basis of $Q:=M(n)/W$, with weights $n,n-2,\dots,-n$, each occurring once; in particular $Q$ is finite-dimensional and nonzero with a one-dimensional $n$-weight space. By [F7] every composition factor of $M(n)$ is $L(n)$ or $L(-n-2)$, and $L(n)$ occurs exactly once. The simple $L(-n-2)=M(-n-2)$ is infinite-dimensional, because the PBW basis $\{f^kv_{-n-2}:k\ge0\}$ of $M(-n-2)$ is infinite by [F2]; hence no composition factor of the finite-dimensional module $Q$ is $L(-n-2)$, and the only remaining factor is $L(n)$, occurring once. Therefore $Q\cong L(n)$, and $M(n)$ has exactly the two composition factors $L(n)$ and $L(-n-2)$, each once.

**The projective structure.** The block $C_n=\{n,-n-2\}$ is a finite downward-closed ideal with maximum $n$; by [F4] the Verma $\Delta(n)=M(n)$ is projective in the block. Every submodule is a sum of weight spaces: polynomial interpolation in $h$ extracts the finitely many weight components of any vector. If a submodule contains $v_k$ for $0\le k\le n$, then $e^kv_k$ is a nonzero multiple of $v_0$ by step 1.2, and the submodule is all of $M(n)$. Thus every proper submodule lies in $W=\operatorname{span}\{v_k:k\ge n+1\}$, whose quotient is $L(n)$ by step 3.1; $W$, rather than all lower weight spaces, is the unique maximal submodule. A submodule mapping onto $L(n)$ contains a weight-$n$ vector and hence $v_0$, so $M(n)\twoheadrightarrow L(n)$ is essential. By uniqueness of projective covers [F5], $P(n)=P(e\cdot l)$ is isomorphic to $\Delta(n)$ and is the projective cover of $L(n)$. For the other label apply BGG reciprocity [F6]: $(P(-n-2):\Delta(n))=[M(n):L(-n-2)]=1$ and $(P(-n-2):\Delta(-n-2))=[M(-n-2):L(-n-2)]=1$ by steps 2.1 and 3.1, while all other flag multiplicities vanish since the block has only these two labels. So $P(s\cdot l)=P(-n-2)$ has a flag with the two factors $\Delta(n)$ and $\Delta(-n-2)$, each once. If its quotient factor were $\Delta(n)$, projectivity of $\Delta(n)$ would split that two-step flag, contradicting the indecomposability of $P(-n-2)$ in [F5]. Hence the submodule factor is $\Delta(n)$ and the quotient factor is $\Delta(-n-2)$, giving the short exact sequence $0\to\Delta(n)\to P(-n-2)\to\Delta(-n-2)\to0$. This sequence is nonsplit: a splitting would exhibit $P(-n-2)\cong\Delta(n)\oplus\Delta(-n-2)$ as a direct sum of two nonzero objects, contradicting the indecomposability of projective covers in [F5]. Finally $\Delta(-n-2)=M(-n-2)=L(-n-2)$ by step 2.1.

**The multiplicity data for $n=0,1$.** The four flag multiplicities of the Example are those just computed and do not depend on $n$: $(P(e\cdot l):\Delta(e\cdot l))=1$, $(P(s\cdot l):\Delta(e\cdot l))=1$, $(P(s\cdot l):\Delta(s\cdot l))=1$, $(P(e\cdot l):\Delta(s\cdot l))=0$ (the last because $P(n)\cong\Delta(n)$ has only the factor $\Delta(n)$). The composition multiplicities are likewise independent of $n$: $[M(n):L(n)]=[M(n):L(-n-2)]=[M(-n-2):L(-n-2)]=1$ and $[M(-n-2):L(n)]=0$ by steps 2.1 and 3.1, since $M(-n-2)=L(-n-2)$ is simple and its highest weight differs from $n$. For $n=0,1$ these are exactly the displayed matrices; they match $P_{e,e}=P_{e,s}=P_{s,s}=1$, $P_{s,e}=0$ by [F10], as asserted by the multiplicity theorem on the A page.

**The transported sequence.** Take the principal block $n=0$ and the target $n=1$, both dominant regular integral, and note that for $\lambda=0$, $\mu=1$ the difference $\mu-\lambda=1$ has dominant member $\nu=1$; here $E=L(1)$ is the two-dimensional simple with weights $+1,-1$, each once, and $E^*\cong E$. By [F9] the tensor $E\otimes M(0)$ has Verma flag factors $M(1)$ and $M(-1)$, and $E\otimes M(-2)$ has factors $M(-1)$ and $M(-3)$. The projections to the blocks $\chi_1$ and $\chi_0$ keep exactly the factors lying in the respective dot orbits $\{1,-3\}$ and $\{0,-2\}$ by [F1]: hence $F(M(0))=\operatorname{pr}_{\chi_1}(E\otimes M(0))\cong M(1)$ and $F(M(-2))\cong M(-3)$, while $G(M(1))=\operatorname{pr}_{\chi_0}(E\otimes M(1))\cong M(0)$ from the factors $M(2),M(0)$ and $G(M(-3))\cong M(-2)$ from the factors $M(-2),M(-4)$. By the transport theorem [F8] $F(L(0))=L(1)$, $G(L(1))=L(0)$, $F(P(0))=P(1)$, $F(P(-2))=P(-3)$ and conversely. Since $F$ is exact, applying it to the nonsplit sequence $0\to M(-2)\to M(0)\to L(0)\to0$ of the principal block produces the exact sequence $0\to F(M(-2))\to F(M(0))\to F(L(0))\to0$, that is $0\to M(-3)\to M(1)\to L(1)\to0$ in the block $C_1$; it is nonsplit because an exact inverse equivalence $G$ would carry a splitting of its image back to a splitting of the original sequence. The original middle module is $M(0)=P(0)$, not $P(-2)$; it is indecomposable by step 1.2, and its submodule $M(-2)$ and quotient $L(0)$ are both nonzero by steps 2.1 and 3.1, so such a splitting is impossible.

The claims of the Example are therefore all verified: the two blocks $C_0$ and $C_1$ share the displayed multiplicity matrices (steps 4.1 and 5.1), the projective cover $P(e\cdot l)$ equals $\Delta(e\cdot l)$ and $P(s\cdot l)$ carries the nonsplit two-step sequence with $\Delta(s\cdot l)=L(s\cdot l)$ (step 4.1), the character identities telescope to the Weyl character of the $(n+1)$-dimensional simple (step 2.2), and the actual inverse equivalences $F$ and $G$ transport the principal-block Verma sequence to $0\to M_{-3}\to M_1\to L_1\to0$ (step 5.2). The two blocks use different weight series; only the labels and the combinatorial data agree.

citations.quote:
Fix a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$ of type
$A_{n-1}$ with Cartan $\mathfrak h$, positive system $\Phi^+$, Weyl vector
$\rho$, Weyl group $W$ (identified with $S_n$) and dot action
$w\cdot\lambda=w(\lambda+\rho)-\rho$. Fix a dominant regular integral weight
$\lambda$, i.e. $\langle\lambda+\rho,\alpha^\vee\rangle\neq0$ for every root and
$\lambda$ integral, and let $\mathcal O_\lambda$ be the corresponding regular
integral block in the conventions of
[[def-regular-integral-category-o-block-and-its-antidominant-weight]]: standard
objects $\Delta(w\cdot\lambda)=M(w\cdot\lambda)$, simples $L(w\cdot\lambda)$,
indecomposable projectives $P(w\cdot\lambda)$ for $w\in W$, with
$\lambda=e\cdot\lambda$ the unique dominant and $w_0\cdot\lambda$ the unique
antidominant element and $\Delta(w_0\cdot\lambda)=L(w_0\cdot\lambda)$.

This item freezes the following conventions, each inherited from the cited
suppliers and used verbatim below.

(i) **Multiplicity conventions.** $(P(w\cdot\lambda):\Delta(y\cdot\lambda))$ is
the Verma-flag multiplicity of [[def-verma-flag-and-its-multiplicities]] and
$[M(y\cdot\lambda):L(w\cdot\lambda)]$ the composition multiplicity, and
$$(P(w\cdot\lambda):\Delta(y\cdot\lambda))=[M(y\cdot\lambda):L(w\cdot\lambda)]$$
by BGG reciprocity ([[thm-bgg-reciprocity]]).

(ii) **Bruhat reversal convention.** Along the bijection
$W\ni w\mapsto w\cdot\lambda$ the Bruhat order runs opposite to the dominance
order, in the two exact senses used on this page: $y\le w$ implies
$w\cdot\lambda\le y\cdot\lambda$ in the dominance order, and every nonzero
multiplicity forces the index direction, i.e.
$[M(y\cdot\lambda):L(w\cdot\lambda)]\neq0$ implies $y\le w$ in the Bruhat
order. The first sense is the inclusion direction of
[[lem-dominant-integral-dot-translates-embed-in-the-verma-module]] (for
$w\ge y$ one has $M(w\cdot\lambda)\subseteq M(y\cdot\lambda)$, so the highest
weight of the submodule is the lower one), and the second is
[[lem-jordan-holder-factors-of-verma-modules-lie-above-the-head]], which
confines every composition factor of $M(y\cdot\lambda)$ to labels
$w\ge y$. The full statement that the two orders are isomorphic as posets is
not needed here and is not asserted; only these two directions, together with
the finiteness of intervals of the Bruhat order
([[lem-bruhat-order-basic-properties-for-permutations]]), are used.

(iii) **Hecke and Kazhdan–Lusztig normalization.** The Kazhdan–Lusztig basis
$\underline H_w=\sum_{y\le w}p_{y,w}H_y$ of the normalized type-$A$ Hecke
algebra ([[thm-existence-and-uniqueness-of-the-kazhdan-lusztig-basis]]), with
$$p_{y,w}=v^{\ell(w)-\ell(y)}P_{y,w}(v^{-2})$$
in the classical $q=v^{-2}$ normalization
([[def-kazhdan-lusztig-polynomials-in-the-classical-q-normalization]]), support
$p_{y,w}=0$ unless $y\le w$, diagonal $p_{w,w}=1$, and simultaneous inversion
symmetry $p_{y^{-1},w^{-1}}=p_{y,w}$.

(iv) **Soergel label and character dictionary.** Write $R_x$ for the
polynomial standard graph bimodule supported at $x$, and $B_x$ for the
normalized indecomposable polynomial Soergel bimodule, which is generally not a
standard graph bimodule. With right reduction $\bar B=B\otimes_S\mathbb C$
and left coinvariant-module values of $V$, the projective dictionary is
$$V(P(w\cdot\lambda))\cong\bar B_{w^{-1}}$$
([[thm-indecomposable-projectives-correspond-to-indecomposable-soergel-modules]]).
The graph label $x$ corresponds to the standard
$\Delta(x^{-1}\cdot\lambda)$. The individual support ranks are measured on the
polynomial lift before reduction, as in
[[prop-verma-flag-multiplicities-are-standard-filtration-ranks-under-v]];
no separated graph-support filtration of the reduced module is asserted.

For degree bookkeeping use precisely the standard-generator normalization of
[[def-type-a-standard-graph-bimodules-support-filtrations-and-character]]:
$\Delta_x(d)=R_x(d-\ell(x))$, and $r_{x,d}(B)$ counts these normalized polynomial
standard layers. Thus the coefficient polynomial is
$$m_x(B;v):=\sum_d r_{x,d}(B)v^d,\qquad h_\Delta(B)=\sum_xm_x(B;v)\widetilde T_x,\qquad\widetilde T_x=v^{\ell(x)}T_x.$$
Here $\widetilde T_x$ is the normalized **standard** Hecke element $H_x$ used
in clause (iii) and
[[def-normalized-type-a-hecke-algebra-and-its-bar-involution]]. The published
Soergel split-Grothendieck-ring convention instead names its simple
Kazhdan--Lusztig generators $H_i=v(T_i+1)=\widetilde T_{s_i}+v$; these must not
be confused with the standard element $H_{s_i}=vT_i$
([[thm-split-grothendieck-group-of-the-soergel-category-is-the-type-a-hecke-algebra]]).
The standard-character supplier
[[lem-the-type-a-standard-character-is-multiplicative]] identifies $h_\Delta$
with that split-Grothendieck-ring isomorphism. This records the coefficient
normalization, and does not infer the image of a general indecomposable $B_x$
by multiplying simple generators. In particular the character theorem must be
used to identify $h_\Delta(B_x)$ with $\underline H_x$; a product of simple
Soergel classes is a Bott--Samelson class and need not be $[B_x]$.
The inverse labels and all rank comparisons above use auxiliary polynomial
gradings only; forgetting them gives the ordinary projective dictionary.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mathfrak g$ be a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra with Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$, a chosen positive-root system and corresponding Borel, Weyl group $W$, and half-sum $\rho$ of positive roots. Let $\chi_\lambda$ and $\chi_\mu$ be the central characters obtained from highest weights $\lambda,\mu\in\mathfrak h^*$ for this Borel. Then

$$\chi_\lambda=\chi_\mu \quad \text{if and only if} \quad \mu\in W\cdot \lambda,$$

where $W\cdot \lambda:=\{w(\lambda+\rho)-\rho : w\in W\}$.

For $\lambda\in\mathfrak h^*$, the **Verma module** is the induced
$\mathfrak g$-module

$$M(\lambda):=U(\mathfrak g)\otimes_{U(\mathfrak b)}\mathbb C_\lambda,$$

where $U(\mathfrak g)$ is the quotient algebra of
[[def-universal-enveloping-algebra-as-a-tensor-quotient]] and
$\mathbb C_\lambda$ is [[def-one-dimensional-borel-module-of-weight-lambda]].
Write $v_\lambda:=1\otimes c_\lambda$.  Thus $M(\lambda)$ is the quotient of
$U(\mathfrak g)$ by the left ideal generated by $x$ for $x\in\mathfrak n^+$
and $h-\lambda(h)$ for $h\in\mathfrak h$; in particular,
$\mathfrak n^+v_\lambda=0$ and $hv_\lambda=\lambda(h)v_\lambda$.

Multiplication gives a vector-space isomorphism

$$U(\mathfrak n^-)\xrightarrow{\sim}M(\lambda),\qquad u\longmapsto uv_\lambda.$$

Consequently, ordered negative-root PBW monomials from
[[thm-pbw-ordered-monomial-basis-for-the-enveloping-algebra]] applied to
$v_\lambda$ form a basis.

Assume the Axiom of Choice.

If $\langle\lambda+\rho,\alpha^\vee\rangle<0$ for every $\alpha\in\Phi^+$, then $M(\lambda)$ is simple. Thus every regular antidominant weight, in this explicit sense, has simple Verma module.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $\Gamma$ be a
finite downward-closed ideal of a linkage class $C$
([[def-truncated-category-o-at-a-finite-weight-ideal]]) and let
$\lambda\in\Gamma$ be maximal in $\Gamma$. Then $\Delta(\lambda)=M(\lambda)$
is a projective object of the truncation $\mathcal O_\Gamma$
([[def-projective-object]]).

More precisely, for every $X\in\mathcal O_\Gamma$ evaluation at the
highest-weight generator $v_\lambda$ is a natural isomorphism
$\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal O_\Gamma}(M(\lambda),X)\to
X^{\mathfrak n^+}_\lambda=X_\lambda$, and $X\mapsto X_\lambda$ is exact, so
$\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal O_\Gamma}(M(\lambda),-)$ is exact.

Under the fixed positive-Borel convention the essential hypothesis is
maximality of $\lambda$ in the finite ideal $\Gamma$: maximality, not any
antidominance or sufficient-positivity condition, is what makes every
$\lambda$-weight vector singular. For a weight $\lambda$ that is not maximal
in $\Gamma$, $\Delta(\lambda)$ need not be projective in $\mathcal O_\Gamma$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Every simple object
$L(\mu)$ of $\mathcal O$ admits a projective cover
$P(\mu)\twoheadrightarrow L(\mu)$
([[def-essential-epimorphism-and-projective-cover]]), which may be chosen
inside the linkage class of $\mu$; the cover is unique up to isomorphism and
indecomposable. Consequently $\mathcal O$ has enough projectives: every object
of $\mathcal O$ is a quotient of a finite direct sum of such projective
covers, because objects of $\mathcal O$ have finite length and each composition
factor is a quotient of its projective cover.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). For all weights
$\lambda$ and $\mu$,
$$(P(\lambda):\Delta(\mu))=[\Delta(\mu):L(\lambda)]=[M(\mu):L(\lambda)],$$
where $P(\lambda)$ is the projective cover of $L(\lambda)$, the left-hand
multiplicity is the Verma-flag multiplicity of
[[thm-projectives-in-category-o-have-verma-flags]], and the right-hand
multiplicity is the simple composition multiplicity of the Verma module
$M(\mu)$ ([[def-standard-and-costandard-objects-in-category-o]]).

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $\lambda\in\Lambda^+$ and $w\in W$. If a simple module $L(\mu)$ occurs in a composition series of $M(w\circ\lambda)$, then $\mu=u\circ\lambda$ for some $u\ge w$ in Bruhat order; moreover $L(w\circ\lambda)$ occurs exactly once. Consequently every composition factor of $M(w\circ\lambda)$ has length at least $\ell(w)$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Work in category
$\mathcal O$ with the conventions of the preceding definitions. For a weight
$\lambda$ write $\chi_\lambda$ for the generalized central character obtained
from $\lambda$, so that $\chi_\lambda=\chi_\mu$ if and only if
$\mu\in W\mathbin\cdot\lambda$
([[cor-central-characters-are-dot-weyl-orbits]]), and let
$\mathcal O=\bigoplus_\chi\mathcal O_\chi$ be the central-character
decomposition of [[thm-category-o-decomposes-by-generalized-central-character]]
with inclusions $\operatorname{incl}_\chi$ and exact projections
$\operatorname{pr}_\chi$, so that
$\operatorname{pr}_\chi\circ\operatorname{incl}_\chi=\operatorname{id}$.

For a finite-dimensional $\mathfrak h$-semisimple $\mathfrak g$-module $E$
([[def-weight-and-weight-space-of-a-lie-algebra-representation]]) and two
generalized central characters $\chi,\chi'$, set
$$T_{\chi,E,\chi'}:=\operatorname{pr}_{\chi'}\circ(E\otimes-)\circ\operatorname{incl}_\chi\colon\mathcal O_\chi\longrightarrow\mathcal O_{\chi'}.$$
This is well defined because $E\otimes-$ is an exact endofunctor of
$\mathcal O$
([[prop-tensoring-with-a-finite-dimensional-module-preserves-category-o]])
and the projections and inclusions are exact.

For weights $\lambda,\mu$ with $\mu-\lambda$ integral
([[def-dot-action-facets-and-single-wall-translation-data]]), let $\nu$ be the
unique dominant weight in the linear Weyl orbit $W(\mu-\lambda)$, which exists
and is unique by [[lem-finite-weyl-closed-chambers-and-stabilizers]] and is
integral; let $L(\nu)$ be the finite-dimensional simple module of highest
weight $\nu$
([[thm-finite-dimensional-simple-modules-are-classified-by-dominant-highest-weights]]).
Define
$$T_\lambda^\mu:=T_{\chi_\lambda,L(\nu),\chi_\mu}\colon\mathcal O_{\chi_\lambda}\longrightarrow\mathcal O_{\chi_\mu},\qquad T_\mu^\lambda:=T_{\chi_\mu,L(\nu)^*,\chi_\lambda}\colon\mathcal O_{\chi_\mu}\longrightarrow\mathcal O_{\chi_\lambda},$$
where $L(\nu)^*$ is the ordinary linear dual, a finite-dimensional
$\mathfrak h$-semisimple simple module isomorphic to $L(-w_0\nu)$ by
[[prop-highest-weight-of-the-dual-representation]].

The labels $\lambda$ and $\mu$ denote actual weights and not $\rho$-shifted
parameters. The central-character subcategories used here are those of the
published decomposition; a central-character summand can contain several
linkage blocks of
[[thm-central-character-summands-split-into-linkage-blocks]], while for an
indecomposable central-character summand the present functors are translation
between that summand and its target.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\lambda,\mu$ be dominant regular integral
weights for the same complex type-$A$ semisimple Lie algebra and fixed positive
system. Let $\nu$ be the unique dominant member of $W(\mu-\lambda)$ and
$E=L(\nu)$ the finite-dimensional simple. The actual translation functors
$$F=T_\lambda^\mu=\operatorname{pr}_{\chi_\mu}(E\otimes-)\operatorname{incl}_{\chi_\lambda},\qquad G=T_\mu^\lambda=\operatorname{pr}_{\chi_\lambda}(E^*\otimes-)\operatorname{incl}_{\chi_\mu}$$
are exact mutually inverse equivalences, with natural adjunction isomorphisms
$\operatorname{Id}\cong GF$ and $FG\cong\operatorname{Id}$. They preserve the
dot-orbit labels: for every $w\in W$,
$$F\Delta(w\cdot\lambda)\cong\Delta(w\cdot\mu),\quad FL(w\cdot\lambda)\cong L(w\cdot\mu),\quad FP(w\cdot\lambda)\cong P(w\cdot\mu),$$
and conversely for $G$. Consequently the two blocks have identical Verma-flag
and composition multiplicities, both equal to $P_{y,w}(1)$, and $F$ transports
the inverse-Kazhdan–Lusztig character identity as a Grothendieck-group identity
with the same signed weighted-inverse coefficients $q'_{w,x}(1)$ and the same
support $x\ge w$. Formal characters in the two blocks use their respective
weights $x\cdot\lambda$ and $x\cdot\mu$; they need not be equal as weight
series. The dominant/antidominant, Bruhat, left/right and inverse-Soergel-label
conventions are preserved. This is an ungraded categorical transport and
supplies no Ext or Koszul grading.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $E$ be a
finite-dimensional $\mathfrak h$-semisimple $\mathfrak g$-module with weight
multiplicities $\dim E_\eta$
([[def-weight-and-weight-space-of-a-lie-algebra-representation]]). For every
weight $\mu$, the object $E\otimes\Delta(\mu)$ has a finite Verma flag
([[def-verma-flag-and-its-multiplicities]]) whose factors are $\Delta(\mu+\eta)$,
the factor $\Delta(\mu+\eta)$ occurring $\dim E_\eta$ times; the factors can be
ordered so that a real-linear height $\ell$ with $\ell(\alpha_i)=1$ is nonincreasing.

Consequently, if $X\in\mathcal O$ has a finite Verma flag with multiplicities
$(X:\Delta(\nu))$, then $E\otimes X$ has a finite Verma flag and
$$(E\otimes X:\Delta(\mu))=\sum_\eta\dim E_\eta\,(X:\Delta(\mu-\eta)).$$

Identify $\mathbb Z[q]$ with $\mathbb Z[v^{-2}]$ by $q\mapsto v^{-2}$. For $y\le w$ in $S_n$, put $d=\ell(w)-\ell(y)$ and define the **Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomial** $P_{y,w}(q)\in\mathbb Z[q]$ by $$P_{y,w}(v^{-2})=v^{-d}p_{y,w},$$ where $\underline H_w=\sum_{y\le w}p_{y,w}H_y$ is the Kazhdan–Lusztig basis of [[thm-existence-and-uniqueness-of-the-kazhdan-lusztig-basis]]. The parity clause of that theorem makes the right side a polynomial in $v^{-2}$. The conventions are: $P_{y,w}=0$ unless $y\le w$, $P_{w,w}=1$, $P_{y,w}$ has constant term 1, and for $y<w$ its degree is at most $(\ell(w)-\ell(y)-1)/2$. The **$\mu$-coefficient** is $$\mu(y,w):=	ext{coefficient of }q^{(\ell(w)-\ell(y)-1)/2}	ext{ in }P_{y,w},$$ defined to be 0 when $\ell(w)-\ell(y)$ is even; equivalently $\mu(y,w)$ is the coefficient of $v$ in $p_{y,w}$. One writes $\mu(y|w)
e0$ when $y
e w$ and ($y<w$ and $\mu(y,w)
e0$) or ($w<y$ and $\mu(w,y)
e0$). The dictionary with the literature is recorded for use: with the classical parameter $T_s^2=(q-1)T_s+q$ one has $H_w=v^{\ell(w)}T_w$, the element $\underline H_w$ is the basis element $C'_w$ of [EW], and $h_{y,w}=p_{y,w}$ with $v^{\ell(w)-\ell(y)}P_{y,w}(v^{-2})=h_{y,w}$ [EW, Remark 3.2].

Assume the Axiom of Choice. In a regular integral type-$A$ block
$\mathcal O_\lambda$, for every $w\in W$ the class of $L(w\cdot\lambda)$ in the
Grothendieck group, equivalently its formal character, is
$$[L(w\cdot\lambda)]=\sum_{x\in W}q'_{w,x}(1)\,[M(x\cdot\lambda)],\qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad \mathrm{ch}\,L(w\cdot\lambda)=\sum_{x\in W}q'_{w,x}(1)\,\mathrm{ch}\,M(x\cdot\lambda),$$
where $q'_{x,w}$ are the inverse Kazhdan–Lusztig coefficients of
[[def-inverse-kazhdan-lusztig-polynomials]] ($Q'=P^{-1}$, $q'_{x,w}\in v\mathbb Z[v]$
for $x<w$, $q'_{w,w}=1$) and the sum is supported on $x\ge w$. Equivalently, in
the signed normalization $q_{x,w}=\mathrm{sgn}(x)\mathrm{sgn}(w)q'_{x,w}$ the
formula is the signed inverse-Kazhdan–Lusztig sum
$$\mathrm{ch}\,L(w\cdot\lambda)=\sum_{x\ge w}(-1)^{\ell(w)-\ell(x)}q_{w,x}(1)\,\mathrm{ch}\,M(x\cdot\lambda).$$
The coefficients $q'_{w,x}(1)$ are the weighted incidence-algebra inverse of
$(P_{y,z}(1))$, given by the finite signed chain sum of products of
$P_{y,z}(1)$; they are integers that may be negative. They specialize to
ordinary Bruhat Möbius values on intervals where every comparable-pair
Kazhdan–Lusztig value is $1$, but not in general. Only the value at $q=1$
occurs.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). For every dominant
integral weight $\lambda\in\Lambda^+$, the character of the finite-dimensional
simple module $L(\lambda)$ is
$$\operatorname{ch}L(\lambda)=A(\lambda+\rho)\cdot A(\rho)^{-1}=\Bigl(\sum_{w\in W}(-1)^{\ell(w)}e^{w(\lambda+\rho)}\Bigr)\Big/\Bigl(e^{\rho}\prod_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}(1-e^{-\alpha})\Bigr),$$
the quotient being taken in the completed character ring $\mathcal R$ of
[[def-completed-formal-character-ring-for-downward-cones]], where
$A(\rho)$ is invertible with inverse
$e^{-\rho}\prod_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}(1-e^{-\alpha})^{-1}$
([[thm-weyl-denominator-identity]],
[[lem-geometric-series-invertibility-in-the-completed-character-ring]]). No
quotient of ordinary functions is intended before this formal cancellation is
justified.

derivations.claim: **The two blocks.** With $\rho=1$ the dot action on coordinates is $s\cdot l=s(l+1)-1=-l-2$, so the orbit of $n$ is $\{n,-n-2\}$; a weight $l$ is dominant regular integral exactly when $l\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}$, and then $-n-2<n$ in the dominance order. Hence $C_n$ is a regular integral block with the two labels $e=123\mapsto n$ and $s=213\mapsto-n-2$; for $n=0$ and $n=1$ the abstract labelled data are the same, which is what makes the two blocks directly comparable.

**The PBW computation.** Fix $n\ge0$ and put $v_k:=f^kv_n$, a basis of $M(n)$ by [F2]; the highest weight vector $v_0$ generates $M(n)$ and spans the $n$-weight space, which is one-dimensional. From the $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ relations $[h,f]=-2f$, $[e,f]=h$ one computes $h\cdot v_k=(n-2k)v_k$, $f\cdot v_k=v_{k+1}$, and, by induction on $k$ from $e\cdot v_0=0$, $e\cdot v_k=k(n-k+1)v_{k-1}$. If $M(n)=A\oplus B$ with $v_0=a+b$, then $a$ and $b$ lie in the one-dimensional weight space $M(n)_n=\mathbb Cv_0$; if $b\ne0$ then $b$ is a nonzero multiple of $v_0$, so $v_0\in B$ and $M(n)=U(\mathfrak g)v_0\subseteq B$, while if $b=0$ then $v_0=a\in A$ and $M(n)\subseteq A$; either way one of the summands is zero. So $M(n)$ is indecomposable.

**The submodule $W$.** Let $W:=\operatorname{span}\{v_k:k\ge n+1\}$. By step 1.2 it is stable under $f$ and $h$; and $e\cdot v_{n+1}=(n+1)(n-(n+1)+1)v_n=0$, while for $k\ge n+2$ one has $e\cdot v_k=k(n-k+1)v_{k-1}$ with $k-1\ge n+1$, so $e$ maps $W$ into $W$. Hence $W$ is a nonzero submodule. Its highest weight vector $v_{n+1}$ has weight $n-2(n+1)=-n-2$ and is killed by $e$; the linear map $M(-n-2)\to W$ sending the basis element $f^kv_{-n-2}$ of the PBW model of $M(-n-2)$ to $v_{n+1+k}$ is a $\mathfrak g$-module isomorphism by the action formulas of step 1.2 (both sides have the same $h$-eigenvalues and the same $e,f$-action). Since $-n-2+1=-n-1<0$, the Verma $M(-n-2)$ is simple by [F3], so $W\cong M(-n-2)=L(-n-2)$.

**Characters.** By step 1.2 the weight multiplicities of $M(n)$ are $1$ in each weight $n-2k$, $k\ge0$, so $\mathrm{ch}\,M(n)=\sum_{k\ge0}e^{n-2k}$ and $\mathrm{ch}\,M(-n-2)=\sum_{k\ge0}e^{-n-2-2k}$; the character formula of [F10] therefore gives $\mathrm{ch}\,L(n)=\mathrm{ch}\,M(n)-\mathrm{ch}\,M(-n-2)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}e^{n-2k}=e^{n}+e^{n-2}+\cdots+e^{-n}$, in agreement with the Weyl character of the finite-dimensional simple $L(n)$ by [F11], and $\mathrm{ch}\,L(-n-2)=\mathrm{ch}\,M(-n-2)$.

**The quotient is $L(n)$.** By step 1.2 the images of $v_0,\dots,v_n$ form a basis of $Q:=M(n)/W$, with weights $n,n-2,\dots,-n$, each occurring once; in particular $Q$ is finite-dimensional and nonzero with a one-dimensional $n$-weight space. By [F7] every composition factor of $M(n)$ is $L(n)$ or $L(-n-2)$, and $L(n)$ occurs exactly once. The simple $L(-n-2)=M(-n-2)$ is infinite-dimensional, because the PBW basis $\{f^kv_{-n-2}:k\ge0\}$ of $M(-n-2)$ is infinite by [F2]; hence no composition factor of the finite-dimensional module $Q$ is $L(-n-2)$, and the only remaining factor is $L(n)$, occurring once. Therefore $Q\cong L(n)$, and $M(n)$ has exactly the two composition factors $L(n)$ and $L(-n-2)$, each once.

**The projective structure.** The block $C_n=\{n,-n-2\}$ is a finite downward-closed ideal with maximum $n$; by [F4] the Verma $\Delta(n)=M(n)$ is projective in the block. Every submodule is a sum of weight spaces: polynomial interpolation in $h$ extracts the finitely many weight components of any vector. If a submodule contains $v_k$ for $0\le k\le n$, then $e^kv_k$ is a nonzero multiple of $v_0$ by step 1.2, and the submodule is all of $M(n)$. Thus every proper submodule lies in $W=\operatorname{span}\{v_k:k\ge n+1\}$, whose quotient is $L(n)$ by step 3.1; $W$, rather than all lower weight spaces, is the unique maximal submodule. A submodule mapping onto $L(n)$ contains a weight-$n$ vector and hence $v_0$, so $M(n)\twoheadrightarrow L(n)$ is essential. By uniqueness of projective covers [F5], $P(n)=P(e\cdot l)$ is isomorphic to $\Delta(n)$ and is the projective cover of $L(n)$. For the other label apply BGG reciprocity [F6]: $(P(-n-2):\Delta(n))=[M(n):L(-n-2)]=1$ and $(P(-n-2):\Delta(-n-2))=[M(-n-2):L(-n-2)]=1$ by steps 2.1 and 3.1, while all other flag multiplicities vanish since the block has only these two labels. So $P(s\cdot l)=P(-n-2)$ has a flag with the two factors $\Delta(n)$ and $\Delta(-n-2)$, each once. If its quotient factor were $\Delta(n)$, projectivity of $\Delta(n)$ would split that two-step flag, contradicting the indecomposability of $P(-n-2)$ in [F5]. Hence the submodule factor is $\Delta(n)$ and the quotient factor is $\Delta(-n-2)$, giving the short exact sequence $0\to\Delta(n)\to P(-n-2)\to\Delta(-n-2)\to0$. This sequence is nonsplit: a splitting would exhibit $P(-n-2)\cong\Delta(n)\oplus\Delta(-n-2)$ as a direct sum of two nonzero objects, contradicting the indecomposability of projective covers in [F5]. Finally $\Delta(-n-2)=M(-n-2)=L(-n-2)$ by step 2.1.

**The multiplicity data for $n=0,1$.** The four flag multiplicities of the Example are those just computed and do not depend on $n$: $(P(e\cdot l):\Delta(e\cdot l))=1$, $(P(s\cdot l):\Delta(e\cdot l))=1$, $(P(s\cdot l):\Delta(s\cdot l))=1$, $(P(e\cdot l):\Delta(s\cdot l))=0$ (the last because $P(n)\cong\Delta(n)$ has only the factor $\Delta(n)$). The composition multiplicities are likewise independent of $n$: $[M(n):L(n)]=[M(n):L(-n-2)]=[M(-n-2):L(-n-2)]=1$ and $[M(-n-2):L(n)]=0$ by steps 2.1 and 3.1, since $M(-n-2)=L(-n-2)$ is simple and its highest weight differs from $n$. For $n=0,1$ these are exactly the displayed matrices; they match $P_{e,e}=P_{e,s}=P_{s,s}=1$, $P_{s,e}=0$ by [F10], as asserted by the multiplicity theorem on the A page.

**The transported sequence.** Take the principal block $n=0$ and the target $n=1$, both dominant regular integral, and note that for $\lambda=0$, $\mu=1$ the difference $\mu-\lambda=1$ has dominant member $\nu=1$; here $E=L(1)$ is the two-dimensional simple with weights $+1,-1$, each once, and $E^*\cong E$. By [F9] the tensor $E\otimes M(0)$ has Verma flag factors $M(1)$ and $M(-1)$, and $E\otimes M(-2)$ has factors $M(-1)$ and $M(-3)$. The projections to the blocks $\chi_1$ and $\chi_0$ keep exactly the factors lying in the respective dot orbits $\{1,-3\}$ and $\{0,-2\}$ by [F1]: hence $F(M(0))=\operatorname{pr}_{\chi_1}(E\otimes M(0))\cong M(1)$ and $F(M(-2))\cong M(-3)$, while $G(M(1))=\operatorname{pr}_{\chi_0}(E\otimes M(1))\cong M(0)$ from the factors $M(2),M(0)$ and $G(M(-3))\cong M(-2)$ from the factors $M(-2),M(-4)$. By the transport theorem [F8] $F(L(0))=L(1)$, $G(L(1))=L(0)$, $F(P(0))=P(1)$, $F(P(-2))=P(-3)$ and conversely. Since $F$ is exact, applying it to the nonsplit sequence $0\to M(-2)\to M(0)\to L(0)\to0$ of the principal block produces the exact sequence $0\to F(M(-2))\to F(M(0))\to F(L(0))\to0$, that is $0\to M(-3)\to M(1)\to L(1)\to0$ in the block $C_1$; it is nonsplit because an exact inverse equivalence $G$ would carry a splitting of its image back to a splitting of the original sequence. The original middle module is $M(0)=P(0)$, not $P(-2)$; it is indecomposable by step 1.2, and its submodule $M(-2)$ and quotient $L(0)$ are both nonzero by steps 2.1 and 3.1, so such a splitting is impossible.

The claims of the Example are therefore all verified: the two blocks $C_0$ and $C_1$ share the displayed multiplicity matrices (steps 4.1 and 5.1), the projective cover $P(e\cdot l)$ equals $\Delta(e\cdot l)$ and $P(s\cdot l)$ carries the nonsplit two-step sequence with $\Delta(s\cdot l)=L(s\cdot l)$ (step 4.1), the character identities telescope to the Weyl character of the $(n+1)$-dimensional simple (step 2.2), and the actual inverse equivalences $F$ and $G$ transport the principal-block Verma sequence to $0\to M_{-3}\to M_1\to L_1\to0$ (step 5.2). The two blocks use different weight series; only the labels and the combinatorial data agree.
